explain.say: Heat always flows from warm to cold, so in winter it leaks out of a warm house through the walls, roof, floor and windows. In an uninsulated house about a third escapes through the walls and about a quarter through the roof.

explain.say: Many houses have an outer brick wall and an inner wall with a gap, or cavity, between them. Filling that cavity with insulation can cut the heat lost through the walls by around two thirds.

faq.q: Why does heat escape from a house?
faq.a: Heat always flows from warmer places to colder ones. It conducts through walls, roofs and windows, and warm air leaks out through gaps, carrying heat with it.
asks: Where does a house lose its heat?

faq.q: How does insulation stop heat escaping?
faq.a: It traps lots of still air in tiny pockets. Air is a poor conductor of heat, and when it cannot move it cannot carry heat by convection, so heat passes through very slowly.
asks: Why is trapped air a good insulator?

faq.a: Many houses built since the 1920s have two walls with a gap between them. Installers drill small holes and blow in mineral wool, beads or foam to fill the gap, then fill the holes.
asks: How is cavity wall insulation put in?

faq.q: How thick should loft insulation be?
faq.a: In Britain the recommended depth for mineral wool loft insulation is about 270 millimetres. Many older homes have much less, so topping it up is a quick, cheap saving.
asks: How much loft insulation do I need?

faq.a: Two panes of glass with a sealed gap of air or argon gas between them slow heat flow, much as a cavity wall does. It roughly halves the heat lost through windows compared with single glazing.

facts: In a typical uninsulated home, around a third of the heat is lost through the walls and about a quarter through the roof.
The recommended depth of mineral wool loft insulation in Britain is about 270 millimetres.
